name: Lori Trahan
stance: Co-author of the bipartisan draft framework with frontier-model safety duties and temporary preemption; says it should be only a start.

statements.text: The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day.
Said the Obernolte-Trahan framework should be only the start and argued for placing AI safety work in the Commerce Department in the open.
Co-introduced the bipartisan FRONTIER Act with Rep. Obernolte, setting transparency, auditing and catastrophic-risk reporting duties for the most advanced AI.
This is how we protect the public from catastrophic risks without slowing the innovation that keeps America competitive
One of ten signers of the bipartisan leadership letter urging Congress to act on AI oversight, security and transparency.

Instead of protecting our kids from the obvious dangers posed by AI, Trump is going to try to block all state laws that have been passed to limit the harms of this emerging technology. This is a handout to Big Tech.
Joined a bipartisan group of 34 House members demanding the White House confront the cybersecurity threat posed by advanced AI models.

There’s no federal law on the books governing how the most powerful AI systems in the world are built, tested or deployed. No independent auditors verify their safety claims. No federal agency has clear authority to step in when something goes wrong.
Released, with Rep. Jay Obernolte, a discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act to establish accountability for the most powerful AI systems.
We need a national strategy that prioritizes safety and national security at the federal level while ensuring states can protect their residents from AI harms.
Without a comprehensive federal strategy on AI, the most powerful corporations will set their own rules.
Responded to a critique that the whistleblower section of the Trahan-Obernolte discussion draft was flawed, saying her office would take a look.
The question isn't whether Congress should act. It's whether we will act in time.
I released a bipartisan discussion draft to create a federal AI strategy that will keep the most powerful AI models safe, protect American workers and make sure our innovators lead the world.

AI models will only grow more capable, and the glaring risks will only grow with them. But without a federal strategy, power will continue to concentrate in the hands of companies racing to build the most potent technology in human history.

Decisions this consequential shouldn’t turn on a single directive issued at 5pm on a Friday. They should follow rules that are clear, fair, grounded in technical facts, and built to last beyond any one administration.
Without a national strategy on AI, even more power will concentrate in the hands of the largest corporations.
We can’t make the same mistake with AI. We need a bipartisan national framework that puts Americans’ safety and livelihoods first.
We need a real national strategy. Agencies staffed with technical experts, uniform guardrails for frontier models, and a lawful process for emergency action that answers to judicial review.
The most powerful AI companies aren’t waiting for Washington to catch up. They’re racing ahead developing even more powerful models, and the risks are growing with them.
Introduced the FRONTIER Act with Rep. Jay Obernolte to require transparency and independent oversight of the largest AI developers under a single national standard.

Last week a powerful AI model broke out of a sealed testing environment, got onto the open internet, and hacked into another company’s live systems. All on its own. Right now, there’s no law on the books to know when that could happen or require companies to disclose when it does.
Americans are worried about AI's catastrophic risks and are counting on Congress to take decisive action.
There's alarming AI news nearly every week, and the risks only grow as more powerful models are built.
1,100+ people building AI just signed a statement warning it could soon move beyond our ability to control it. When the builders sound the alarm, Congress should listen.
Endorsed Sen. Amy Klobuchar's push to reach agreement on the Thune-Klobuchar AI framework over August ("I agree.").
Independent audits. Transparency & mandatory incident reporting. A hand on the switch if something goes wrong.

For the second time this month, an AI model broke into real companies during a safety test. Anthropic disclosed it today after OpenAI did the same last week. We can’t run AI safety on the honor system.
When it comes to the most powerful AI models and the risks they pose, we can't rely on an honor system.
Voluntary transparency isn't enough.
AI governance belongs in a civilian agency, where it can be seen and questioned, not buried inside the national security apparatus. Secrecy by default doesn’t make us safer.
AI models are growing more powerful every day and the people building the technology are asking for Congress to set clear guardrails on safety, transparency and preventing catastrophic risk.
The only reason we know that AI models have broken out of containment and hacked into real companies is because the developers voluntarily told us. That has to change.
Boeing doesn't decide on its own whether a plane is safe to fly. Drug companies don't approve their own trials. AI labs shouldn't be the only ones checking their own work either.
Artificial intelligence is moving faster than ever, and the risks are growing with it. Meanwhile, the builders of this technology are begging for guardrails.
Congress has a duty to protect Americans from the catastrophic risks of advanced AI, including potential cyberattacks, development of biological threats, or large-scale harm.
Powerful AI is being built right now with almost no federal oversight.
The FRONTIER Act is the strongest AI safety legislation ever introduced.
My FRONTIER Act would require immediate disclosures and embed independent auditors at the labs so they can detect a catastrophe and the government can intervene to stop it.
Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway.
This will keep happening. The models keep getting more powerful, and nothing but the honor system is holding AI companies accountable.

Top AI researchers and developers are resigning and warning that these companies are only worried about racing to the top and developing the most powerful models as fast as possible. One thing is clear: We can't rely on AI companies to police themselves.
But a voluntary commitment can be dropped the second it gets inconvenient.
Led, with Rep. Don Beyer, a bipartisan request to House leaders of both parties to pass guardrails on advanced AI systems as soon as possible rather than wait out a 53-day recess.
Joined Rep. Yassamin Ansari and more than two dozen House Democrats in urging President Trump to take urgent action on the risks of frontier AI.
A 53-day recess is unacceptable. Families across America don’t get a recess from the high cost of groceries, gas, healthcare, or the risks of AI. Neither should Congress.
Massachusetts families deserve the strongest protections from the risks posed by powerful AI models.
When someone breaks the law and hurts you, you can take them to court. That shouldn't change just because the wrongdoer is an AI agent.
My CLAIM Act makes sure people harmed by rogue AI aren’t left without recourse.
Advanced AI systems can now uncover serious vulnerabilities in the code that underpins the internet. That capability can strengthen our defenses, but it can just as easily be turned against us.
Hopefully this reporting is mandatory in the near future, but until then it's entirely reasonable for AI companies to keep Congress apprised as we work on much needed oversight.

But what Republican members of this committee did find time to do last week – in the middle of the night by the way – is force through an unprecedented giveaway to the tech industry: A ten-year ban on state laws that could make AI safer for our constituents.
There's much more to do, including giving CAISI the authority to create the standards we need to know whether a frontier model is safe before it ships, not after something goes wrong.
It establishes uniform transparency and incident reporting, and emergency authority to stop a catastrophe before it happens.
Developers have already built systems capable of acting on their own and causing real damage. The CLAIM Act makes sure they answer for what their systems do.
